newsitem.title: LIBERIA: African military chiefs endorse Liberia polls.
newsitem.headline: African military chiefs endorse Liberia polls.

text.p: West African military chiefs said on Tuesday they were satisfied that the security situation in Liberia was adequate for the conduct of elections in the war-ravaged nation in May as planned.

A meeting of army chiefs decided to recommend to regional foreign ministers holding talks on Thursday that elections should be held on schedule, Nigerian chief of defence staff Major-General Abdul-Salam Abubakar told a news conference.

"Basically what we are recommending is the provision of security and disarmament and the going ahead with the elections," he said after a two-day review of disarmament of rebels under accords ending seven years of civil war.
"We hope the election programme and all other programmes will be maintained as scheduled. This is our recommendation," Abubakar added.

The commander of the ECOMOG peacekeeping force in Liberia, General Victor Malu, told the meeting on Monday disarmament had largely been completed, although his force needed more troops for tactical deployment in populated areas ahead of elections.
"We have just completed the disarmament and demobilisation phases," he said.
Malu said the Nigerian-led force sent to Liberia in 1990 by the Economic Community of West African States was turning its foucus to elections, the final stage of the peace programme.

Diplomats said that while there were still isolated cases of armed attacks and harassment in parts of the country, ECOMOG appeared in control overall and the security situation was expected to improve further before the poll time.
"I think the disarmament exercise was more successful than many people expected," U.S. ambassador William Milam told Reuters on Monday.
"We all believe that while security is not perfect, it is going to get much better," said Milam, whose country has historic ties to Liberia, a nation founded by freed American slaves in 1847.

The United States, the European Union, the United Nations and other agencies have stepped up logistics and material support for ECOMOG since an explosion of ethnic warfare in Monrovia last April nearly torpedoed the peace process.
Washington expects to spend up to $6 million to assist the organisation of elections.

U.N. and independent poll experts are less optimistic about the organisation of free and fair elections by May. But suggestions of a delay have sparked fierce opposition from Liberia's chief warlord Charles Taylor.
Taylor launched the civil war that has killed more than 150,000 people since December 1989 but has now disarmed his guerrillas and says he expects to be elected president.
